# Review Rules — graduated lessons (auto-generated)

> Generated by `scripts/kb/regenerate.mjs` from `dev-cycle-analytics/review-lessons.jsonl`.
> Do not edit by hand. These are recurring code-review findings that recurred often
> enough to graduate into always-loaded project rules. Honor them when writing code.

## security

- **Validate inputs against an allowlist at the persistence/trust boundary.** Reject any key or enum value not on a known-good allowlist (recursively for nested bodies) inside the write function itself, never via a guessed denylist or compile-time-only TypeScript union; runtime allowlisting is what protects integrity when a future caller passes request-supplied values.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #125/#127 (a denylist of eight content key names let query/transcript and nested {key:...} through) and #154 (addReviewEvent inserted whatever event string it received, with the audit vocabulary enforced only by TS at call sites).
- **Security gates must fail closed and validate at runtime.** An authorization/approval gate must reject any unrecognized value (fail-closed), validate the value with a runtime allowlist rather than a compile-time union, and be inverted so the permissive branch is the only explicitly named one.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #152 (the publish gate used positive equality gate === 'required-approval', so any typo or unvalidated route param fell through and published with no approval check).
- **Range-validate numeric/threshold config on both bounds.** Validators at a trust boundary must enforce upper bounds, integrality, and semantic ranges (not just finite-and-non-negative), and clamp privacy-protecting thresholds to a hard floor; checking only the lower bound lets an admin value exhaust resources or silently disable a safety guard.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #107 (baselineWindow:100000000 the engine iterates per scan), #123 (rejectThreshold:50 / aiSignatureThreshold:0 made 'struggling' unreachable), and #159 (minSample:1 with no floor could expose one developer).

## correctness

- **Keep user-supplied values disjoint from reserved keys and sentinels.** Namespace dynamic object keys built from user-controlled names (e.g. prefix t:) so a value can't shadow a structural key, and never overload one string param to mean both a real identifier and a sentinel; thread an explicit discriminated scope instead.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #104 (a team named 'date' overwrote the chart x-axis when written as row[team.name]) and #124 (getTeamPRReviewCoaching used scope:string for both a team name and the 'org' sentinel).
- **Bound and clamp ranges driven by external timestamps.** Any loop or window filter whose extent derives from stored/client timestamps must be bounded on both ends: clamp the upper edge to now, cap window length, and never let a single future-dated or skewed row explode the series or inflate counts past a privacy floor.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #106 (buildTrajectory walked week-by-week to max(lastActivity, now), emitting thousands of zero-weeks from one future-dated snapshot) and #132 (loop/nudge aggregates filtered detected_at >= cutoff with no upper bound).
- **A teardown route needs the same in-flight guard as the routes it races.** A destructive/teardown route must take the same in-flight overlap guard as the mutating routes it races with. Fire-and-forget runs apply their deferred writes at the END of the run, keyed by something other than the row being deleted and with no re-check that the row still exists — so a delete accepted mid-run is silently undone minutes later by the settling run, restoring exactly the state the teardown removed. Reject with a typed 409 while a run is in flight (or make the deferred writes re-verify their target still exists); note that 'the thing is misbehaving' is the likeliest reason someone reaches a delete endpoint, so the race is the common case, not the exotic one.
  - _Why:_ #262: DELETE /api/admin/git/providers/:id purged the container's cursors with no activeSyncs check, unlike POST /:id/sync and /:id/sync-older-history which both guard on it. A sync-now run's cursorAdvances closures write git_last_sync/git_earliest_sync unconditionally when the run settles, so deleting during a long first sync purged the cursors and had them rewritten minutes later.
- **Docs, config keys, and parity claims must match the code.** Verify every documented config key against the actual loader (loaders silently ignore unknown keys), and never justify a change by claiming it 'mirrors' another module unless that module actually does the same thing; note deliberately out-of-scope alignments.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #108 (docs said dashboard_base_url but the key is dashboard_url, yielding Slack alerts with no deep link and no error) and #145 (docstrings claimed parity with Pillar 3 cohort resolution, which actually filters by per-developer opt-in, not team-level exclusion).
- **A completion signal is not a currency claim.** When a cap, chunk, or bound makes 'the run completed' stop implying 'the data is current', the operator surfaces must distinguish the two and report the new in-between state — the run that succeeds while the data is still months old is exactly the one an operator reads as an all-clear. Never infer a positive health claim from narrower checks returning empty: state only what was measured, or add a positive check for the claim you want to make. Partition exclusions must key on the underlying state, not on a display threshold — a condition held below its reporting threshold still falsifies the opposite claim.
  - _Why:_ #235: a catch-up cap created 'complete run, cursor still 170 days back'. Right after excluding the repo that caused a stall, the streak cleared and doctor printed 'All N provider(s) advancing' while ~170 days of snapshots were still missing. The added lag signal then keyed its stall-exclusion on the >=3 REPORTING threshold, so a provider held 1-2 runs was printed as 'catching up - advancing' while its cursor was in fact held; and the all-clear was inferred from both readers being empty, which is not evidence of currency.
- **A remedy printed to an operator is executable advice — verify it is reachable and safe.** Before an error/advisory string tells an operator HOW to fix something, verify the instruction against the code three ways. (1) Is it SAFE? Trace it through the invariants — an instruction the codebase documents elsewhere as corrupting (purging a sync cursor over retained additive rows, re-importing a non-disjoint window) is worse than saying nothing, because the operator trusts it more than their own judgement. (2) Is it REACHABLE for every provenance the message can be emitted under? A route that 409s config-file entities, or a cascade that short-circuits while another owner still resolves, makes the named repair a no-op that looks like a fix. Say so explicitly rather than naming a remedy that half the deployments cannot run. (3) Is it COMPLETE? If the repair resets state to a bounded default (a first-sync window, a retention floor), the recovery step for everything outside that bound is part of the remedy, not an optional extra.
  - _Why:_ #280: the advisory told the operator to reset the provider's cursors and re-import — the exact operation the #262 rule documents as re-arming a permanent double-count, and a far larger corruption than the understatement being repaired. The corrected remedy then had two more holes: the admin delete route refuses config-file providers outright and the cascade is skipped while the YAML entry owns the container, and re-adding restores only the 6-month first-sync window, silently dropping older history.
- **A timestamp compared as a string must be shape-pinned, and its bounds must be total.** If a stored timestamp is ever compared with string operators (>=, ORDER BY) rather than parsed instants, pin its shape at the trust boundary with an anchored regex — a toISOString() round-trip is NOT enough, because ISO 8601 expanded/negative years ('+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z') round-trip cleanly yet sort before ordinary years and invert every comparison. Make each bound total: compare parsed instants, and reject an unparseable operand explicitly instead of letting NaN compare false and fall through the guard. Where a tighter bound is already provable from state the function has loaded (e.g. a floor can never exceed the forward cursor), prefer it over a looser one like 'before now'.
  - _Why:_ #233: the declared history floor is compared lexically against the stored watermark by the backfill's overlap guard, but the validator accepted any value that round-tripped through toISOString(). '+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' passed, and since '+' (0x2B) sorts below '2' (0x32) it read as 'in the past', slipped the upper bound, and bricked the provider's backfill permanently. The same guard also let an unparseable `now` pass, because NaN >= NaN is false.

## over-abstraction

- **Reuse the canonical helper instead of cloning shared logic.** Before hand-rolling SQL/math, a gate check, a row decoder, preference plumbing, a duplicate column, or visibility resolution, find the existing canonical helper and reuse or extract it; a second copy (or a hardcoded flag literal, or a duplicate stored value) creates a second source of truth that silently drifts.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #104 (re-derived tier/trend SQL), #107 (re-implemented override gate by hardcoding the flag), #122/#126/#130/#131 (byte-for-byte copied period-walk/decode/coerce/preference plumbing), #123 (rework_rate duplicate column), and #155 (re-implemented visibility orchestration and forked a quieter row decoder).
- **Don't build scope without a real production caller.** Build exactly what the issue's acceptance criteria require: do not add config knobs, precedence chains, alternate code paths, network transports, scoring algorithms, runtime predicates/guards, or layered wrapper functions whose only callers are tests or their own definitions; defer the seam until a real consumer exists.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #102 (speculative per-team overrides and percentageBaseline mode), #125/#127 (uncalled RealtimeCoach config and httpCaptureTransport), #154 (a 3-line rule fractured into uncalled wrappers and read helpers), #157 (90 LOC of a sibling task's scoring), #159 (test-only options object), and #162 (test-only SCOLDING_WORDS blocklist/isEncouraging predicate).

## performance

- **Resolve sets in one query; no per-row fan-out or full scans.** Resolve cohort/membership/hidden-id sets once with a single JOIN/query before any loop and do in-memory checks inside, and fetch a single entity with a point-read plus the shared visibility check; never run O(N) per-row DB round-trips or scan the whole visible set and JS-filter to one row on every request.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #132 (org opt-in resolution fired ~D×(3+2·prefs) synchronous queries), #161 (the pinned-practice loop re-ran the hides query per id), and #163 (loadVisiblePractice scanned all visible practices and .filter(...)[0] on every detail/history/feedback request).

## testing

- **Test every failure path, mode, edge, and budget that can actually trip.** Size perf assertions to a realistic org, cover documented edges/boundaries and >=2-item degenerate cases (not just the single-item happy path), exercise both branches of dual-mode components and every exposed query filter, add a failing-hook rollback test for each distinct transaction shape, and assert server DTO mapping by seeding real data and reading it back through the API rather than a frontend fixture.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #108/#105/#106 (the <2s perf test ran on ~5 developers and edge/boundary cases had zero coverage), #152 (rollback was tested only for publish() not the submit() auto-publish path), #162 (the DTO test asserted only four fields), and #163 (the editor's edit path and the browse 'team' filter were untested).
- **Assertions must be able to fail against the real leak vector.** Every negative/privacy assertion must match a string or shape the code actually emits, with a seeded positive control that produces the signal; decode BLOB columns to strings before scanning for forbidden plaintext (JSON.stringify serializes Buffers as integer arrays), and drive sanitizers/security controls through the real execution path (e.g. the actual MATCH query), not just their returned string.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #133 (assertions checked capital-Y 'You were active', an id substring with no carrying field, and BLOB markers invisible because Buffers serialized to integer arrays), #155 (FTS-injection safety was asserted only on the builder's returned string), and #162 (the test relied on a hand-built frontend fixture that cannot catch a server mapping error).
- **A stricter guard needs the input class that only it handles.** When you replace a guard with a stricter or more total form — `=== undefined` to `Array.isArray`, a truthiness check to an explicit shape test, a two-state check to a three-state one — the existing fixtures were written for the looser form and almost never contain an input the two forms disagree on. So the added strictness ships with no test that can fail, and the next reviewer who calls it redundant is right on the evidence available. Add the input class that ONLY the new form handles (the non-array, the null, the NaN) and verify by experiment that reverting the guard fails exactly that test and nothing else. Do not let the justification live only in a comment: a comment cannot fail CI, and a comment that also overstates what the check inspects (a container test is not element validation) is worse than none.
  - _Why:_ #271: the sync loop's reuse guard was hardened from `rawCommit.diffs === undefined` to `Array.isArray(rawCommit.diffs)` so a non-array from a provider adapter would fall back rather than read as 'this commit touched nothing'. A reviewer verified that reverting it passed all 658 git tests — absent, `[]` and populated all behave identically under `!== undefined`, so the one branch the code argued hardest for was the one branch no fixture could distinguish.

## data-integrity

- **An additive merge may only sum genuinely-disjoint deltas; combine re-delivered data idempotently.** Before converting a REPLACE upsert into an additive merge, prove each field's per-run value is a DISJOINT delta. Fields sourced from a window re-fetched by updated_at/updated_on (e.g. PRs, and their re-fetched review comments) are re-delivered on every subsequent sync, so additively summing them double-counts permanently. Add only truly-disjoint deltas (e.g. commit committer-date windows); combine re-delivered fields idempotently (max, or recompute from an idempotent source table), and commit-count-weight rate/score fields so a small delta can't drag a large accumulated row toward a plain mean.
  - _Why:_ #205: switching git_snapshots to an additive merge fixed commit-drop but would have inflated prs_opened/prs_merged/review_comments_given on every scheduled sync (providers fetch PRs by updated_at, so an active PR is re-fetched and re-aggregated each run). Resolved by max() for PR/review fields and commit-weighted averages for rates.
- **Check and store the same normalized value.** A uniqueness/existence guard must be handed the SAME normalized string the write persists. If the guard trims (or lowercases, or canonicalizes) and the write stores the raw value, the identifier that was proved free is not the identifier that was claimed: the stored value resolves nothing forever, and a later honest claim of the normalized form still looks free — so two rows nominally own one identity.
  - _Why:_ #255: findIdentityConflict trimmed github/bitbucket/gitlab before findByExternalId, but addDeveloper was handed the untrimmed input. '--github " alice"' passed a lookup for 'alice', stored ' alice', never resolved in buildDevLookupMap, and left 'alice' claimable by a second developer.
- **An idempotent recompute must actually run and retract stale rows.** If correctness relies on idempotent recompute, schedule it across the trailing K periods (with a manual recompute path), and have each per-period recompute DELETE rows for entities no longer in the regenerated set in the same transaction; never write a period once and never touch it again.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #123 (created-at attribution was justified by recompute but only the just-completed period ran, losing late-arriving PR activity, and re-attribution left the old developer's rows intact).
- **Before deleting state, ask which invariant reads it as proof.** Deleting a cursor, watermark, or marker is a data-integrity decision, not hygiene. Before removing one, find every invariant that reads it as PROOF and check whether the proof survives without it. A forward sync cursor is not just 'where this provider got to' — it is the only evidence that the next run's window is disjoint from what is already stored, which is what licenses an additive merge. Forgetting it re-arms a permanent double-count over data the delete deliberately left behind, and data that is keyed by a coarser identity than the thing being deleted (e.g. rows keyed by provider TYPE, not by the provider row) cannot be retracted alongside it. If the retained data cannot be retracted or the merge made idempotent, the state must not be forgotten — say so instead of asserting the merges absorb the overlap.
  - _Why:_ #262: provider delete purged git_last_sync/git_earliest_sync so a re-added provider would honor its first-sync window. But mergeDailyAcrossRuns ADDS commits/lines/files on the stated premise that commit windows are disjoint, upsertRawAuthorDaily has no dedup guard, and raw_author_daily is keyed by provider TYPE — so delete + re-add + re-sync would permanently double every commit metric in the re-imported span, and git_snapshots (a pure projection) would propagate it. The issue's out-of-scope note asserted the merges were idempotent; they are idempotent only for the max()-combined PR/review fields.
- **Validate entity existence and lifecycle state before a write.** Before writing a flag, endorsing/ranking, or appending an audit/outcome row, fetch the target and assert it exists and is in the expected lifecycle/precondition state (returning a typed not_found/not_published error, not a raw DB error), and require FK or existence/canonicalization checks on actor and functional-key columns; a non-blank check alone lets a typo/ghost id write a row that silently does nothing.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #157 (endorsePractice/orderPracticePool acted on draft/removed rows and surfaced a raw SQLITE_CONSTRAINT), #126 (recovery/complete logged unconditionally without a matching open initiate), and #151/#154 (audit actor/author ids had no FK and a mis-cased team recorded a hide that hid nothing yet 'succeeded').
- **Wrap read-modify-write and multi-statement writes in a transaction.** Any read-then-write that preserves omitted fields, or any check-then-act/multi-statement mutation (including MAX(version)+1), must run inside a single db.transaction; a UNIQUE backstop turns a race into a fail-fast error, it does not serialize.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #156 (setPracticeDetails did a non-atomic read-merge-UPSERT) and #151 (addContributionVersion computed MAX(version)+1 in a deferred tx with a doc overstating collision safety).
- **A scoped/single-source write into a multi-source-aggregated row must merge, not replace.** When a row aggregates contributions from multiple sources under one key (e.g. git_snapshots keyed (developer, day) merging all providers), any write that runs over a SUBSET of sources must additively merge against the stored row; a full-column REPLACE upsert from a scoped run silently drops the other sources' same-day contribution. Prefer merge-on-conflict, or document the caveat and forbid the scoped path in multi-source deployments.
  - _Why:_ #192: per-provider Sync-now (and CLI sync git --provider) ran runSync over one provider and the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET ... = excluded.* rewrote the merged multi-provider day-row from just that provider's data; incremental cursors meant the loss persisted until a state reset.
- **Resolve at the same grain the decision is actually made at.** When a derived view answers a question that the write/projection path decides PER ROW (is this attributed? does this resolve?), it must resolve at that same grain. Do not roll rows up to one identity first (MAX/GROUP BY over a mutable column) and resolve the collapsed value: if the rollup picks the resolving variant the unresolved rows are silently hidden, and if it picks the non-resolving one the count includes rows already accounted for elsewhere. Group by the full identity tuple, resolve each variant, then fold only the ones that matter.
  - _Why:_ #254: listAuthorCandidates resolved distinctRawAuthors' MAX(author_email) rollup, but the projection resolves each raw row's own (login, email) and sync stamps one run's sample commit email onto every date row that run writes. An author committing from two addresses was therefore either dropped from the review queue while half their history projected to nobody, or listed with a commit_count including already-attributed commits (which auto-create would turn into a duplicate developer).

## determinism

- **Make ordering correct, total, and deterministic.** Order semantic enums by an explicit numeric rank (CASE/rank map) not lexically; make comparators total (never NaN, sort missing rows to a stable extreme rather than coalescing to a real value); and break ties on a monotonic insertion key (rowid), never a random UUID.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #102 (ORDER BY severity DESC on a text column sorted lexically, burying the highest severity last), #105 (metrics coalesced to NEGATIVE_INFINITY made two no-data rows compare as NaN), and #160 (a same-millisecond pin tiebreak on a random UUID resolved nondeterministically).

## api-contract

- **Keep the client/server wire contract in sync.** Type a wire field with the same breadth the source guarantees (narrow an unconstrained TEXT column with a safe default rather than asserting a closed union the data doesn't enforce), and when a response shape changes, update every consumer to narrow on the new field before dereferencing, plus its test mock.
  - _Why:_ Recurred in #105 (an unconstrained TEXT ai_maturity_basis was cast to a closed union on the frontend) and #131 (the backend wrapped pr-coaching in {enabled,...} but the client still dereferenced data.all_pr and the stale mock masked the TypeError).
